full_judgment:
37. The Muhammadan law does not recognise legitimation and acknowledgment cannot create or confirm the status of a legitimate son in favour of or upon a person, who as a matter of a fact, is not or is disproved to be the legitimate son of the acknowledged. But in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, an acknowledgment raises a presumption, the rebuttal of which is the burden of the person who disputes it and such a presumption can be rebutted only on the proof that the acknowledged person is not or cannot be the legitimate son of the acknowledger. 

 The acknowledgment may be repudiated by the acknowledge. But if none of those objections occur, then the acknowledgment has more than a mere evidential value. It raises a presumption of marriage a presumption which may be taken advantage of either by a wife claimant or a son claimant. Being, however, a presumption of fact, and not juris et de jure, it is, like every other presumption of fact, capable of being set aside by contrary proof. 

 39. Mr. Khondker, Counsel for the appellants, placed the Allahabad Judgment in full as well as the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the privy Council in the case of Saddique Hossain Khan vs. Hashem Ali Khan (43 IA 212) before us and also made lengthy submissions on the principle stated therin, but it appears that the High Court has correctly enunciated the law as to the acknowledgment being substantive proof of legitimacy and having the effect of raising the presumption of legitimacy. The finding of fact that the respondent could not prove that he was the legitimate son of the deceased Mutwalli, based as it is on a wrong view of law as to the effect of acknowledgment in establishing legitimacy in Muslim law was, therefore, correctly reversed by the High Court. 

 40. The principle which seems to be well established is that an acknowledgment has the effect of raising presumption of legitimacy excepting where illegitimacy is proved beyond doubt by reason of the marriage of its parents being either disproved or found to be unlawful. Having regard to this principle the High Court came to the conclusion that prima facie, in view of the earlier acknowledgment by Amir Ali, respondent should be accepted as the legitimate eldest son of Amir Ali until the contrary is proved in a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction and that as such the respondent had better claim to be appointed as a Mtuwalli under Section 43 of the Ordinance, The High Court did not, it appears, arrive at any conclusive finding on the question but held that on the correct view of law respondent shall be presumed to be the eldest son till such presumption was rebutted in a properly framed suit.
